## What is menopause?

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item When menstruation pauses (stops) \pause
\item Officially in menopause when you have gone 12 months without menstruating
\begin{itemize}
\item The time leading up to menopause is called peri-menopause 
\item After the 12-month mark, you are "menopausal" or postmenopausal 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```
## "Symptoms" in Menopause and Peri-menopause

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Referring to the experiences during (peri-)menopause as symptoms is in itself controversial \pause
\begin{itemize}
\item Because menopause is not a "disease" \pause
\item But we will use "symptoms" to describe the physical and mental health experiences attributable to menopause \pause 
\end{itemize}
\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.5\textwidth}
\item diminished sleep quality 
\item insomnia
\item irritability 
\item depression
\item mood swings
\item difficulty concentrating 
\item reduced quality of life 
\item aching joints
\item bloating 
\item breast tenderness 
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.5\textwidth} 
\item bladder/urinary discomfort
\item more frequent urinary tract infections 
\item vaginal dryness, discharge, and bleeding 
\item loss of sexual desire, painful intercourse
\item headaches
\item thinning hair 
\item heart palpitations
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{itemize}
```
## Menopausal Hormone Therapy: History

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item What is (o)estrogen? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Everyone has hormones! Everyone has estrogen(s)-- different types and different quantities \pause 
\item In females, primarily produced in ovaries and placenta (when pregnant); responsible for development and regulation of female reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics \pause
\end{itemize}
\item 1940s: new techniques to extract estrogen from the urine of pregnant mares (female horses); marketed as a treatment for menopausal symptoms in the 1950s \pause
\item 1960s: "Feminine Forever": youth, beauty, full sex life for menopausal women who take estrogen \pause
\item 1970s: Criticism of "paternalistic" medical establishment labeling menopause as a "deficiency disease" when it is a natural part of aging. Argue against using the term hormone "replacement" 
\end{itemize}
```
## Menopausal Hormone Therapy: History

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item 1980s: Progesterone added for women with uterus as estrogen alone increased rates of uterine cancer and endometrial cancer (estrogen alone still used for those without uterus) \pause
\item 1980s-1990s: multiple \textbf{observational} studies suggest hormones (estrogen or estrogen+progesterone) reduce risk of heart disease, reduce development of osteoporosis, might reduce the risk of Alzheimer's, and are the best available treatment for vasomotor symptoms \pause
\begin{itemize}
\item "...estrogen should be in the water... we thought it was like fluoride" -Hadine Joffe, Harvard Medical School professor of psychiatry 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```
## Observational Studies

```{=tex}
\small
\begin{itemize}
\item 1984 National Institutes of Health Consensus Conference on Osteoporosis statement: estrogens most effective means of preventing bone loss \pause 
\item Nurses' Health Study: 1991 observational study of 48,000 postmenopausal women: those who took hormones had a 50\% lower risk of heart disease than those who did not \pause
\item 1996 New York aging study: 1124 elderly women free of Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and stroke; age at onset of Alzheimer's significantly later for those taking estrogen and relative risk significantly reduced compared to non-users \pause 
\item 1998 study of Swedish women aged 50-81 with and without hip fractures; hormone therapy significantly reduces risk of hip fracture, risk of hip fracture decreased by about 6\% for every year of use \pause 
\item Between 1975 and 2000, of twenty published studies examining menopausal hormone therapy, 80\% found no increased risk of breast cancer, 10\% found an increased risk of breast cancer, 10\% found a decreased risk of breast cancer (meta-analysis sponsored by Wyeth) 
\end{itemize}
```
## The Women's Health Initiative

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item under the National Institutes of Health (NIH)
\item Launched in 1993 
\item Aims: test the benefits and risks of hormonal therapies (estrogen or estrogen+progesterone) for chronic diseases \pause

\item 16608 women without hysterectomy (intact uterus) randomized: 8506 assigned to estrogen+progesterone (CEE+MPA), 8102 assigned to placebo \pause 

\item Intervention phase: November 1993-July 2002 \pause 

\item Study halted July 2002 (average follow-up 5.2 years)

\end{itemize}
```
## WHI Halted

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Why did the WHI halt the estrogen+progesterone arm of the study in 2002? \pause \item Increased risks of breast cancer, stroke, heart attack, and clots (pulmonary embolism) \pause 
\item What do we mean by increased risks? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item In 1 year for 10,000 postmenopausal women taking estrogen+progesterone, 8 more will have invasive breast cancer, 7 more will have a heart attack, 8 more will have a stroke, 18 more will have blood clots, than a similar group of 10,000 women not taking the hormones (Dr. Rossouw, acting director WHI)
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```
## WHI Criticized

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item The halt? Internal Validity? External Validity? \pause
\item Criticism of the halt: at the time (July 2002), differences in risks across treatment and control groups not statistically significant \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item How many additional cases of breast cancer is too many? \pause
\end{itemize}
\item Internal validity: \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item No multiple outcomes adjustments, no multiple subgroup comparison adjustments \pause 
\end{itemize}
\item External validity: \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item "healthy women" \pause
\item application of results to peri-menopausal women \pause
\item contextualization of risks 
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```

## Risk as an Estimand

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item The study reports counts and hazard ratios \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Time is a factor (longitudinal): (a) women who did not have breast cancer at t=1 might develop it at t=2 or t=5, (b) any individual's repeated follow-ups are not independent, (c) the numerator at later follow-ups may be different as people die \pause 
\end{itemize}
\item Survival Analysis and Hazard Ratios 
\begin{itemize}
\item Relate time that passes before an event occurs (e.g. breast cancer, stroke, death) to covariates \pause 
\item Among individuals without breast cancer, what is the probability they develop breast cancer in the next year? \pause The paper then pools this over all years into a hazard ratio (HR)
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```
## Risk as an Estimand

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item How do we interpret hazard ratios? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item What if $HR=1$? \pause no difference between the hazard of breast cancer for treatment and control \pause 
\item What if $HR<1$? \pause hazard of breast cancer is lower for treated \pause 
\item What if $HR>1$? \pause hazard of breast cancer is higher for treated \pause
\end{itemize}
\item In 2002, the WHI Data and Safety Monitoring Board calculated an HR of 1.26, a 26\% increase in breast cancer risk under treatment \pause 
\item The WHI and media reporting on the halt of the study have been criticized for failing to communicate the difference between absolute and relative risks ($\frac{8}{10000} \neq .26$)
\end{itemize}
```
## Results from WHI

What is the effect of estrogren+progesterone on invasive breast cancer in post-menopausal women?

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Intervention phase (1993-2002): HR of 1.24 (95\% CI, 1.01-1.53) \pause
\item  Overall, 9 more cases of invasive breast cancer per 10,000 person-years 
\end{itemize}
```
\includegraphics{WHIfig}

## WHIMS

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Prior observational studies suggested hormone therapy could reduce risk of Alzheimer's/cognitive decline or increase age of onset \pause 
\item Who enrolled in WHIMS? \pause WHI 65 to 79 year olds, free of dementia at the time of enrollment \pause 
\item CEE+MPA Arm: 2131 assigned to treatment, 2213 placebo; mean follow-up 4.2 years \pause
\item What is the outcome of interest? \pause Annual measure of 3MSE (cognition test) scored 0 to 100 \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Temporal and spatial orientation, immediate and delayed recall, executive function, naming, verbal fluency, abstract reasoning, writing, copying \pause 
\item Women who scored below cutpoints were given additional testing for dementia (follow ups continued regardless of dementia status)
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
```
## Results from WHIMS

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item  We still have longitudinal challenge \pause 
\item Why is adherence a concern? \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item Non-compliance is always a concern to some extent, but non-compliance here may be directly related to cognitive decline! \pause
\end{itemize}
\item CEE+MPA difference from placebo averaged 0.18 points (SE 0.10) \pause
\item Difference is "too small to have relevance in clinical practice" 

\end{itemize}
```

Why are the results from the pre-WHI literature so different from the WHI(MS) results?

## Recent Observational Studies

```{=tex}
\begin{itemize}
\item Why consider evidence from observational studies? \pause 

\item Recent observational studies look at different formulations/doses, administrations, durations of use, such as: \pause 
\begin{itemize}
\item micronized bioidential progesterones versus synthetic progesterone (MPA)
\item pill/tablets, patches, and injections 
\item durations of use: 1 year or less, 1-3 years, 3 to 6 years, longer than 6 years 
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}
```
